response.message: Kia ora! I'm your pregnancy assistant for Aotearoa New Zealand. I can help you with information about pregnancy, complications, ultrasound scans, care pathways, and support services. How can I help you today?
During pregnancy, your body undergoes remarkable changes to support your growing baby. Here's what you should know:

summary.body: Your body transforms significantly during pregnancy with hormonal changes, increased blood volume, growing uterus, and changes to organs and systems to accommodate and nourish your baby.
summary.placenta: The placenta is a vital organ that connects you to your baby, providing oxygen and nutrients while removing waste. It also produces hormones essential for pregnancy.
summary.fetal: Your baby develops from a single cell to a fully formed human in about 40 weeks, with critical development occurring in the first trimester.
summary.health: Regular checks with your midwife or doctor, including ultrasounds and blood tests, help ensure both you and your baby are healthy throughout pregnancy.
summary.general: Understanding what's happening in your body helps you make informed decisions and recognize when something might need attention.

response.message: While most pregnancies progress smoothly, it's important to understand potential complications. Here's what you need to know:

summary.fgr: Reduced Fetal Growth (FGR) is when a baby doesn't grow as expected in the womb. Regular ultrasounds help monitor growth, and your care team will create a management plan if detected.
summary.preeclampsia: Pre-eclampsia is a condition involving high blood pressure and protein in urine, typically after 20 weeks. Early detection through regular check-ups is crucial for managing this condition.
summary.diabetes: Gestational Diabetes involves high blood sugar that develops during pregnancy. It's manageable through diet, exercise, and sometimes medication. Regular monitoring helps ensure healthy outcomes for you and baby.
summary.general: Pregnancy complications affect about 1 in 10 pregnancies in New Zealand. Early detection and proper care significantly improve outcomes. Your midwife and doctor are your partners in managing any complications.

response.message: Ultrasound is a safe and essential tool for monitoring your baby's health. Here's what you should understand:

summary.what: Ultrasound uses sound waves to create images of your baby. It's completely safe with no radiation, allowing your care team to check on your baby's growth and wellbeing.
summary.doppler: Doppler ultrasound is a special type that measures blood flow through the umbilical cord and baby's organs. It helps detect if your baby is getting enough oxygen and nutrients.
summary.metrics: Ultrasounds measure things like baby's size, amniotic fluid levels, and placental position. Your midwife or doctor will explain what the measurements mean for your pregnancy.
summary.general: Most pregnancies have at least 2 ultrasounds - one at 12 weeks and another at 20 weeks. Additional scans may be needed if concerns arise.

response.message: Understanding pregnancy care in Aotearoa New Zealand helps you know what to expect. Here's what you need to know:

summary.lmc: In New Zealand, you choose an LMC(Leader Maternity Carer) - usually a midwife - who coordinates your pregnancy care from confirmation through to 6 weeks after birth. This care is free under the public health system.
summary.midwife: Most pregnant people in NZ are cared for by midwives who provide continuous, personalized care. They attend your pregnancy check-ups, are present at birth, and provide postnatal support.
summary.pathways: If complications arise, your LMC will refer you to specialist obstetricians or other healthcare professionals. You'll still keep your LMC who works alongside specialists to coordinate your care.
summary.changes: Your care may involve additional specialists if you develop complications like gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, or reduced fetal growth. This ensures you receive appropriate expert care while maintaining continuity.
summary.general: NZ's maternity system is organized around community-based primary care, with hospital specialist services available when needed. This model supports normal pregnancy while ensuring access to expertise when required.

response.message: You're not alone - there are many support services available throughout your pregnancy journey in Aotearoa New Zealand:

summary.universal: All pregnant people in NZ have access to free LMC care, ultrasounds, blood tests, and hospital services. Plunket provides free support for all families with babies and young children.
summary.mental: Organizations like PADA (Perinatal Anxiety & Depression Aotearoa) and Whāraurau provide specialized support for emotional wellbeing during pregnancy and postpartum.
summary.specialist: Additional support is available for specific situations - diabetes clinics, growth restriction monitoring, pre-eclampsia management, and neonatal intensive care.
summary.whanau: Many services offer culturally appropriate care and support for your family/whānau, recognizing the importance of family involvement in pregnancy and parenting.
summary.general: Services are available across all regions of New Zealand. Your LMC can help connect you with local support services relevant to your needs.

response.message: Your mental health during pregnancy and after birth is just as important as your physical health. Here's what you need to know:

summary.importance: Up to 1 in 5 pregnant people experience anxiety or depression. These feelings are common, treatable, and nothing to be ashamed about. Early support makes a real difference.
summary.anxiety: Feeling worried, having racing thoughts, or experiencing panic are signs you may need support. Anxiety during pregnancy is very common and highly treatable with the right help.
summary.depression: Persistent sadness, loss of interest, difficulty bonding with baby, or feeling hopeless are signs to seek help. Depression can occur during pregnancy or after birth.
summary.support: PADA (Perinatal Anxiety & Depression Aotearoa) offers free helpline and resources. Whāraurau provides comprehensive mental health information. Your LMC can also refer you to specialized perinatal mental health services.
summary.general: Talk to your LMC, GP, or call PADA helpline 0800 111 757. Free counselling and support services are available. You deserve support and recovery is possible with the right help.

response.message: Having a premature baby can be overwhelming, but excellent care and support are available. Here's what you should know:

summary.premature: Babies born before 37 weeks are considered premature. About 7-8% of babies in NZ are born prematurely. The earlier a baby is born, the more specialized care they typically need.
summary.nicu: Neonatal Intensive Care Units provide specialized care for premature and sick newborns. They have specialist teams, advanced equipment, and 24/7 monitoring to support your baby's development.
summary.scbu: Special Care Baby Units (SCBU) provide care for babies who need extra support but aren't critically ill. Your baby might need help with feeding, temperature regulation, or monitoring.
summary.support: You can usually stay with your baby, participate in their care (kangaroo care, feeding), and be supported by the neonatal team. Organizations like Little Miracles Trust provide peer support for families.
summary.general: All major hospitals in NZ have neonatal units. Very premature babies may need transfer to a tertiary NICU in larger centers for specialized care.

response.message: Gestational diabetes is manageable with the right care and support. Here's what you need to know:

summary.what: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) occurs when your body can't produce enough insulin during pregnancy, causing high blood sugar. It affects about 5-10% of pregnancies in NZ and usually resolves after birth.
summary.management: Most women manage their blood sugar through healthy eating and regular physical activity. Some may need insulin or medication. Your diabetes team will guide you with a personalized plan.
summary.monitoring: You'll need to check your blood sugar levels regularly (usually 4 times daily) and attend more frequent antenatal appointments. Additional ultrasounds may monitor your baby's growth.
summary.baby: Well-managed GDM usually results in healthy outcomes. Your baby will be monitored after birth to ensure their blood sugar is stable. Breastfeeding helps regulate your baby's blood sugar.
summary.general: Diabetes in pregnancy clinics provide specialist care, dietitian support, and education. Your LMC works with the diabetes team to coordinate your care throughout pregnancy.

response.message: Great question about keeping your baby healthy during pregnancy! Here's what you need to know:

summary.smoking: It's strongly recommended to avoid all smoking and tobacco products during pregnancy. Smoking reduces oxygen supply to your baby and increases risks of premature birth, low birth weight, and developmental issues.
summary.alcohol: No amount of alcohol is considered safe during pregnancy. Alcohol can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders affecting your baby's physical and cognitive development.
summary.nutrition: A balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and dairy is essential. Folic acid (400-800mcg daily) is particularly important for preventing neural tube defects.
summary.exercise: Moderate physical activity like walking, swimming, or prenatal yoga is beneficial. Aim for 30 minutes most days, but always consult your midwife or doctor first.
summary.caffeine: Limit caffeine intake to 200mg per day (about 2 cups of instant coffee or 1 cup of brewed coffee). Excessive caffeine may increase miscarriage risk.
summary.supplements: In addition to folic acid, your midwife may recommend vitamin D, iron, and iodine supplements depending on your individual needs.
summary.general: Your lifestyle choices directly impact your baby's development. Small positive changes can make a big difference in ensuring a healthy pregnancy.

URGENT: This sounds like an emergency. If you're experiencing any of these symptoms, please:

• Call 111 immediately for emergency medical help
• Contact your LMC (midwife or lead maternity carer)
• Go to your nearest hospital emergency department

Don't wait if you're concerned - it's always better to get checked. Your safety and your baby's wellbeing are the priority.
Pregnancy is typically divided into three trimesters over approximately 40 weeks. Here's what happens during each stage:

summary.first: Critical period for baby's development. Major organs form. You may experience morning sickness, fatigue, and frequent urination. First ultrasound around 12 weeks.
summary.second: Often called the 'honeymoon period'. Energy returns, you'll feel baby move (quickening), and have your anatomy scan around 20 weeks. Baby grows rapidly.
summary.third: Final growth phase. Baby gains weight and develops fully. You may experience Braxton Hicks contractions. Prepare for birth and baby's arrival.
summary.general: Your LMC will schedule regular appointments throughout pregnancy to monitor your health and baby's growth. Frequency increases as you approach your due date.

response.message: Baby movements are an important sign of your baby's wellbeing. Here's what you need to know:

summary.when: Most pregnant people first feel baby move between 18-25 weeks (earlier if second pregnancy). Initially feels like flutters or bubbles.
summary.pattern: Baby should have regular patterns of activity. Most active times vary - some babies are night owls! You'll learn your baby's normal pattern.
summary.counting: From 28 weeks, be aware of your baby's usual pattern. You should feel at least 10 movements in 2 hours during baby's active time.
summary.concerns: If you notice reduced or absent movements, or a change from normal pattern, contact your LMC immediately. Don't wait - always get checked.
summary.general: You know your baby best. If something feels different or concerning, always contact your healthcare provider. Never worry about 'bothering' them.

response.message: It's completely normal to have many emotions during pregnancy. Your feelings are valid, and support is available. Here's what can help:

summary.normal: Pregnancy brings huge changes - physical, hormonal, emotional, and life adjustments. Up to 1 in 5 pregnant people experience anxiety or depression. These feelings are common and treatable.
summary.support: If you need someone to talk to now, call PADA helpline 0800 111 757 (24/7). They provide free, confidential support for perinatal mental health.
summary.lmc: Your midwife or doctor is there to support your emotional wellbeing too, not just physical health. They can help connect you with appropriate services.
summary.partners: Don't hesitate to reach out to family, friends, or partner. Building your support network is important for wellbeing.
summary.general: It's normal to feel anxious or down during pregnancy. Free counselling and mental health services are available. Recovery is possible with the right support. You deserve to feel well during this journey.

response.message: Preparing for birth is an important part of your pregnancy journey. Here's what you should know:

summary.options: You can choose hospital birth, home birth, or primary birthing unit depending on your circumstances and local availability. Your LMC will discuss options with you.
summary.plan: Consider your preferences for pain relief, positions, support people, and immediate postnatal care. Discuss these with your LMC to create a flexible plan.
summary.pain: Range from breathing techniques, water immersion, gas and air (Entonox), to epidural. Your options may depend on birth location and circumstances.
summary.classes: Free or low-cost classes help you prepare for labour, birth, and early parenting. Your LMC can recommend local options.
summary.general: While it's good to have preferences, birth can be unpredictable. Trust your care team and your body. The goal is a safe arrival for you and baby.

actions.description: Learn about your LMC's role in birth

response.message: Partners and support people play a vital role during pregnancy, birth, and beyond. Here's how they can help:

summary.pregnancy: Attend appointments with LMC, learn about pregnancy changes, help with healthy lifestyle, provide emotional support, and prepare together for baby's arrival.
summary.emotional: Listen without judgment, acknowledge feelings, help manage stress, and celebrate this journey together. Partners can also experience anxiety - that's normal too.
summary.practical: Help with household tasks, attend antenatal classes, prepare home for baby, learn about newborn care, and plan parental leave.
summary.birth: Be a supportive presence, help with comfort measures, communicate with care team, advocate for birth preferences, and provide encouragement.
summary.general: It's normal to feel anxious or uncertain. Talk to the LMC, attend classes together, and don't hesitate to ask questions or seek support for yourself.
